scenes.title: A structure for finding ideas
lines: Imagine planning an early Pokémon game. Mixing movement, battles, and Poké Ball use in one flat list makes a specific rule hard to find.
We will organize those notes into headings and subordinate details.
We will start with an illustrative Pokémon document, use game menus and move descriptions to learn folding and moving, and then prepare a document for a reader.

scenes.title: Grouping Pokémon planning notes into levels
lines: This is an illustrative planning document based on an early Pokémon game, not an original document from its developer.
Divide the rules into Exploration and Battles. Under Battles, place Move Selection and Item Use. Put the conditions and results for using a Poké Ball together under Item Use.
To revise the catching rule, expand that branch. You can find the related conditions and results together, reducing the risk of mixing them with unrelated rules or overlooking a detail.

scenes.title: From menus to text levels
lines: An outline places smaller items under larger ones to make their grouping visible. Here, a level shows where an explanation belongs, rather than how important it is.
Take the menus in Super Smash Bros. Ultimate. Selecting a main category reveals the choices inside it.
The Vault groups related items such as Sounds, Replays, and Records. The parent sets the scope, while its children divide that scope into more specific parts.

scenes.title: Following the relevant branch
lines: Options contains different choices such as sound, brightness, and language. Inside Sound, the controls distinguish music, sound effects, and voices.
We can organize text the same way: Options at the first level, Sound below it, and sound-effect volume one level deeper.

Indentation makes the relationship visible. Sound and Brightness are peers, while effect volume belongs under Sound. This is an analogy for organizing text, not a claim about the game’s internal code.

scenes.title: From a fighter to move details
lines: Now apply the same approach to a fighter’s moves. The Help menu includes a Move List. Let us use that subject to build a document structure.
In our illustrative document, the levels are Fighter, Special Moves, and an individual move. Under that move, we write its input, action, and result.
How to press the button and what action follows are details of the same move. We are illustrating document structure, not recreating measured game values or Nintendo’s internal design document.

scenes.title: Collapsing and moving a branch
lines: When the move list grows, you do not need to read every detail at once. Collapse the details to scan the headings, then expand them to reveal the same content.
Collapsing does not delete anything; it changes what is visible. To change the order, move the heading together with its subordinate content.
Changing the level changes the grouping. Check whether an item became a peer or moved under another heading. Distinguishing order changes from level changes helps avoid misplaced explanations.

scenes.title: Starting in Word
lines: You do not need to build a special planning tool to try this. In desktop Word, Outline view under the View tab lets you work with document levels.
Assign the main headings and subheadings, display fewer levels to inspect the overall structure, and expand the branch you need.
The controls may differ by program and version. The essential step is assigning the relationship between headings and their content, rather than merely making text larger.

scenes.title: Working notes and a document for others
lines: Once the outline has a structure, consider who will read it. Notes for developing ideas and a document handed to someone else serve different purposes.
Working notes can contain questions that are still unresolved. A document for someone else should make the decisions and the reading path clear.

For the same move, working notes may separate input and result for comparison. A handoff document arranges the headings and explanation for the reader. The organizing tool and the final presentation need not look identical.

scenes.title: Try it with a small list
lines: This method is not limited to game design documents. You can add detailed explanations to video topics, or organize study material and questions.
Try a small list of your own. Place related items under a heading, expand one branch to inspect its details, then collapse it again.
Can you find the explanation you want from the headings alone? If so, you have more than a long list: you have a structure for finding and revising ideas.
